10930: A moveable feast is something (or someone) that is rich, enjoyable, and nourishing — but that changes, shifts, or doesn't stay fixed in one place or time, yet keeps its essential value and pleasure wherever it goes.
Step 1: Understand the Literal Root — Where It Comes From

To understand this idiom, you first need to know what it literally means, because the figurative meaning grows directly out of the literal one.

In the Christian religious calendar, holidays are divided into two types:

Fixed feasts are celebrations that fall on the exact same date every year, no matter what. Christmas is the perfect example — it is always on December 25. It never moves. You can count on it.

Moveable feasts, on the other hand, are religious celebrations whose dates shift from year to year. They are not anchored to a fixed point on the calendar. The most famous example is Easter. Easter doesn't have a permanent date. It is calculated based on the lunar calendar — specifically, it falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox. This means Easter can fall anywhere between late March and late April depending on the year. Other examples of moveable feasts include Ash Wednesday, Good Friday, and Pentecost — they all shift because they are calculated in relation to Easter.

So, in the literal sense, a moveable feast is a celebration that is real, important, and joyful — but unpredictably shifting in time.

That core idea — something wonderful that doesn't stay fixed — is exactly what traveled into the figurative, everyday use of this idiom.
Step 2: How It Became an Idiom

The literal religious meaning laid the groundwork, but the idiom became famous and widely used thanks to Ernest Hemingway, the great American novelist.

Hemingway spent much of the 1920s living in Paris, France, as a young and struggling writer. Paris at that time was electric — full of artists, writers, poets, thinkers, and creative energy. Hemingway soaked it all in. Decades later, he wrote a memoir about that time in his life. He titled it A Moveable Feast, published in 1964 (after his death).

In that book, Hemingway described Paris not just as a city, but as an experience so rich and deeply nourishing that it stayed with him wherever he went for the rest of his life. His famous line captures it perfectly:

"If you are lucky enough to have lived in Paris as a young man, then wherever you go for the rest of your life, it stays with you, for Paris is a moveable feast."

Think about what he meant: Paris wasn't fixed. He left it. He moved on. But the richness of that experience — the conversations, the culture, the growth, the beauty — traveled inside him. It was a feast, not of food, but of life — and it was moveable because it moved with him.

This is the spark that lit the idiom in popular use. After Hemingway, people began using "a moveable feast" to describe any experience, person, or thing that carries this special quality.
Step 3: The Figurative Meaning of the Idiom — Explained Clearly

Today, the idiom "a moveable feast" is used in two closely related but slightly different ways.

Meaning 1 — The Hemingway Meaning (Most Common and Richest):

Something or someone is called "a moveable feast" when they are deeply enriching and pleasurable, and this quality doesn't depend on a fixed place, time, or form — it moves with them, or adapts, or can be found in new shapes. The feast (the richness, the joy, the nourishment) is always there, but it's not locked in one spot.

Think of a brilliant friend who is funny, wise, and warm. Whether you meet them at a café, at a park, or over a phone call — the joy and richness of their company is always there. The feast travels with the person. You might say, "Spending time with her is always a moveable feast — no two conversations are ever the same, but every single one leaves you feeling full."

Meaning 2 — The Practical/Everyday Meaning:

The idiom is also used more plainly to describe something that keeps changing its date, time, or location — usually an event or meeting. Here, the tone is often lighter or even slightly humorous. The focus is less on the richness and more on the moveable part.

For example: "The annual team dinner is a moveable feast — every year it's in a different city, at a different time, and nobody knows when it's happening until two weeks before."

In this usage, "moveable feast" simply highlights that something doesn't have a fixed, predictable slot — it wanders around the calendar or the map.
Step 4: The Core Feeling the Idiom Carries

The key to truly feeling this idiom (not just knowing it) is understanding that it contains two ideas held together at once:

1. A feast — something rich, generous, nourishing, and pleasurable. Not a snack. Not ordinary. A feast implies abundance, depth, and enjoyment.

2. Moveable — not fixed, not anchored, shifting. But importantly, the shifting doesn't reduce the feast. The richness survives the movement. The quality travels.

The idiom is never used for something dull, poor, or mediocre. You would never call a boring meeting "a moveable feast." The feast part always carries a sense of something genuinely worthwhile. The idiom has warmth, appreciation, and even a kind of wonder built into it.
Step 5: Real-World Examples to Lock It In

Here are several examples showing the idiom in action across different situations:

  • "Living in New York for three years was a moveable feast — even though I've moved away, the energy of that city never quite left me."
  • "My grandmother's storytelling is a moveable feast. Whether she's at the dinner table or on a road trip, she always has something that feeds your soul."
  • "The jazz festival is a moveable feast — it's held in a different town every year, but the spirit of it is always the same."
  • "Good literature is a moveable feast. A great novel nourishes you differently at twenty than it does at forty, yet it gives you something each time."
  • "Our project deadline has become a moveable feast — it keeps shifting, and no one knows when it will actually happen."

Notice how in most of these examples, there's a warmth or richness implied. The idiom elevates whatever it's applied to.
Step 6: Tone and Register — When and Where to Use It

This idiom sits in a mid-to-high register. That means:

  • It is not slang. It has a literary, thoughtful, slightly elegant quality to it.
  • It is appropriate in written English (essays, journalism, books, articles) and in spoken English when you want to sound articulate and expressive.
  • It is not used in casual quick conversation the way simpler idioms are. If you use it in everyday speech, it should feel considered and deliberate — and it will sound impressive.
  • It works beautifully in compliments and reflections — when you're describing a rich experience, a wonderful person, or a cherished memory.
Step 7: What This Idiom Is NOT

To avoid confusion, here is what the idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean something negative or chaotic. Changing dates and locations might sound frustrating, but when described as a "moveable feast," the tone is usually neutral-to-positive, not critical.
  • It does not refer to an actual meal (unless used very playfully or literally). The "feast" is always metaphorical — a feast of experience, joy, conversation, richness, or culture.
  • It is not the same as saying something is "unpredictable" in a worrying way. The idiom leans positive. The movement is part of the charm, not the problem.

Literal rootA religious holiday whose date changes each year (like Easter)
Made famous byErnest Hemingway's memoir A Moveable Feast (1964)
Core figurative meaningSomething deeply enriching and pleasurable that changes, shifts, or adapts — yet keeps its essential richness wherever it goes
Secondary meaningSomething that keeps changing its date, time, or location (used more practically)
ToneWarm, literary, appreciative, slightly elevated
Used forPeople, places, experiences, events, relationships — anything with depth and value that is not fixed

The beauty of this idiom is that it carries both a sense of abundance (a feast) and freedom (moveable) at the same time. It is one of those rare idioms that doesn't just describe — it evokes. When you call something a moveable feast, you are saying: this thing is rich and wonderful, and that richness is not trapped in one form or one moment — it lives and moves.
10931:
When you are moved, you feel a deep, strong emotion in response to something — usually something that touches your heart. It is that inner feeling when something beautiful, heartfelt, sad, or profoundly meaningful reaches deep inside you and stirs your emotions.

Think of it as the opposite of being cold or indifferent. When you are moved, something has gotten through to you — past your everyday calm — and stirred something real inside.
What kind of emotion is it?

This is important: "moved" does not describe one single emotion. It describes an emotional state — a deep inner stirring — that can be made up of different emotions depending on the situation.

You can be moved by:

  • Sadness — hearing a story of loss or suffering
  • Gratitude — seeing someone's extraordinary kindness
  • Admiration — watching someone act with great courage
  • Beauty — listening to a breathtaking piece of music
  • Joy and tenderness — watching a child be reunited with a parent
  • Awe — standing in front of a magnificent piece of art

What ties all of these together is depth. Being moved means your emotions were genuinely and deeply stirred — not just a passing feeling on the surface, but something that reached you at a deeper level inside.

Quite strong. "Moved" is not a mild word. It sits above "pleased" or "interested" and closer to "deeply affected." When someone is moved, they have experienced a real emotional impact — it is not casual.

You can intensify it further:

  • "Deeply moved" — even more strongly affected than just "moved." This is one of the most common combinations.
  • "Profoundly moved" — similar to "deeply moved," emphasizing how fundamentally the emotion affected the person.
  • "Visibly moved" — the emotion is apparent to others; you can see it on the person's face or in their behaviour.
What does being moved look like physically?

Because "moved" describes a deep inner emotion, it often shows on the outside. A person who is moved might:

  • Have tears in their eyes or start to cry
  • Get a lump in their throat (a tight feeling that makes it hard to speak)
  • Get goosebumps (skin that prickles from strong emotion)
  • Feel a tightening or ache in the chest
  • Fall silent because words feel insufficient

"Moved to tears"
This means someone was so deeply moved that they cried, or came close to crying. It is an extremely common phrase.
"The audience was moved to tears by her speech."

"Deeply moved" / "Visibly moved"
As described above — these intensify the adjective or tell you that the emotion was clear to others.
"The president was visibly moved during the memorial service."
"I was deeply moved by your letter."

"Moved to do something"
This is a slightly different shade of meaning: here, "moved" means emotionally compelled or inspired to take some action. The emotion was so strong that it led to doing something.
"She was moved to donate all her savings to the cause."
"He was so moved by the suffering he witnessed that he became a doctor."
In this use, the emotion did not just stay inside — it pushed the person to act.
How it differs from similar words

Touched — "Touched" and "moved" are very close in meaning, and people often use them interchangeably. However, "touched" tends to feel slightly softer and gentler — as if the emotion gently landed on you. "Moved" feels deeper and more stirring — as if something shifted inside you.

"I was touched by the card she sent me." (warm, gentle)
"I was moved by the documentary about the refugees." (deeper, more powerful)

Affected — "Affected" is more neutral and clinical. It simply means something had an impact on you, but it does not tell you whether the impact was emotional, positive, or deep. "Moved" is specifically emotional and specifically deep.

Emotional — Calling someone "emotional" describes their general tendency to show or feel emotions strongly. Calling someone "moved" describes a specific response to a specific moment.

Overwhelmed — Stronger than "moved." When overwhelmed, you almost cannot handle the emotion — it is too much. "Moved" is powerful but not necessarily overpowering.

Stirred — Very similar to "moved." Both describe an inner emotional awakening. "Stirred" can sometimes feel more intellectual or idealistic (stirred to think, stirred by an idea), while "moved" tends to feel more purely emotional and heart-centred.

As an adjective, "moved" almost always appears after a linking verb — words like be, feel, seem, look, appear:

  • "She was moved."
  • "He seemed deeply moved."
  • "They felt moved by the performance."
  • "The crowd looked visibly moved."

It can also occasionally appear before a noun, though this is less common:

  • "A moved audience sat in silence."
Putting it all together — examples in context

"When the soldier's daughter ran onto the stage to hug him, everyone in the room was moved."

Here, the reunion stirred the emotions of everyone watching — a mix of joy, tenderness, and perhaps relief.

"She was deeply moved by the kindness strangers had shown her family during the crisis."

The gratitude and warmth she felt was profound — not just "thank you" but something much deeper.

"The film was so powerful that even the director was visibly moved at the premiere."

You could see the emotion on his face — perhaps tears, or a look of being emotionally shaken.

"I was moved to write this letter because I did not want another day to pass without telling you what your friendship has meant to me."

Here, the emotion became the reason for an action — the person felt compelled to write.
The essential idea to carry with you

If you remember one thing: when someone is moved, something has reached deep into their heart and stirred their emotions genuinely and powerfully. It is not a surface-level reaction. Something beautiful, heartfelt, painful, or deeply meaningful has affected them in a real, inner way — and that is what it means to be moved.
10932:
"Movement" means the act or process of moving — a change in position, place, or state. Whenever something shifts from where or what it was, that is movement.

From this one root idea, the word branches out into many different areas of life. Each meaning carries the same core: something is changing, shifting, or progressing.
1. Physical Movement

The most basic meaning: the act of a person, animal, or object changing position or going from one place to another.

  • The movement of the clouds across the sky.
  • The cat froze and watched every movement of the mouse.
  • There was no movement in the dark room — everything was completely still.

It can describe a single action ("a sudden movement") or a general pattern of motion ("the slow movement of traffic").

Notice also that it can describe how something moves, not just that it moves:

  • Her movements were graceful and deliberate. (Here, "movements" means her individual acts of moving — the way she walked, turned, lifted her arms, etc.)
2. Someone's Movements (Whereabouts and Activities)

When you use "movements" in the plural to talk about a person, it means their comings and goings — where they went, what they did, and when, over a period of time.

  • The police tracked the suspect's movements for a week.
  • Can you account for your movements on the night of the crime?
  • Her movements that day were carefully recorded by the security cameras.

This meaning is common in investigations, journalism, and everyday conversation when someone wants to know where a person has been.
3. A Social, Political, or Cultural Movement

This is one of the most widely used meanings in modern life. A "movement" here means a large, organized effort by many people who share a common goal — usually to bring about social, political, or cultural change.

Key features of this kind of movement:

  • It involves many people acting together.
  • It has a shared purpose or cause.
  • It takes place over a period of time (not just a single event).
  • It is usually trying to change something in society.

Examples:

  • The Civil Rights Movement in the United States fought to end racial discrimination.
  • The women's suffrage movement campaigned for women's right to vote.
  • The environmental movement works to protect the planet from pollution and climate change.
  • The independence movement in India sought freedom from British rule.

The word captures something important here: a movement is not just an organization with a name and office — it is a living force of people and ideas pushing in the same direction.
4. A General Trend or Shift

Even without a formal organized group, "movement" can describe a broad shift in how people think, behave, or live — a gradual change in direction.

  • There has been a movement away from processed food toward healthier, home-cooked meals.
  • A growing movement toward remote work has changed how companies are structured.
  • In recent years, there has been a noticeable movement toward minimalism in home design.

The difference from Meaning 3: this use doesn't require an organized group with leaders and campaigns. It can simply describe a drift in collective behavior or preference.
5. A Movement in Art, Literature, or Thought

In art, literature, philosophy, and culture, a "movement" is a shared style, set of ideas, or approach that a group of artists, writers, or thinkers adopt around the same time and place. They may or may not know each other personally, but their work reflects the same spirit.

  • Impressionism was an art movement in 19th-century France, known for its loose brushwork and focus on light.
  • Romanticism was a literary and artistic movement that valued emotion, nature, and the individual.
  • The Beat movement in 1950s America produced writers like Jack Kerouac, who rejected mainstream values.

These movements often have a name, a rough time period, and a recognizable style.
6. A Movement in Music

In classical music, a "movement" is a self-contained section of a larger musical work, such as a symphony, concerto, or sonata. Each movement is like a chapter in a book — it can stand somewhat on its own, with its own mood, tempo, and character, but together with the other movements, it forms a complete whole.

  • Beethoven's Fifth Symphony has four movements.
  • The second movement is slow and gentle, in contrast to the dramatic first movement.
  • Please hold your applause until after all four movements have been performed.

You can think of it this way: the whole symphony is the building, and each movement is a room inside it.
7. A Bowel Movement

In medicine and everyday conversation, "a bowel movement" (often just called "a movement") means the act of passing solid waste from the body through the digestive system.

  • Have you had a bowel movement today? (a doctor might ask this to assess a patient's health)
  • Drinking more water and eating fiber can make movements more regular.

This is a clinical, neutral term — not rude or informal. Doctors, nurses, and parents use it routinely.
8. Movement in Finance and Markets

In economics and finance, "movement" refers to a change in price, value, or rate — how much something has gone up or down.

  • There was significant movement in the stock market today after the announcement.
  • Analysts are tracking the movement of oil prices closely.
  • Any movement in interest rates will affect millions of homeowners.

The word is used here because prices are, in a sense, "moving" — going up or down on a scale.
9. Movement of Troops (Military)

In a military context, "movement" means the deliberate repositioning of soldiers, vehicles, or supplies from one location to another, usually for strategic purposes.

  • The general ordered a movement of troops to the eastern border.
  • Enemy movement was detected near the river.
  • All troop movements were kept secret until the last moment.
10. The Movement of a Clock or Watch

In watchmaking and horology (the study of timekeeping), the "movement" of a clock or watch refers to its internal mechanism — all the gears, springs, wheels, and parts that work together to make it keep time.

  • This watch has a Swiss movement — one of the finest in the world.
  • The jeweler carefully cleaned and oiled the movement inside the antique clock.

The word makes perfect sense here: the little gears and parts are literally moving inside the case.
Bringing It All Together

Every meaning of "movement" connects back to the same idea: things changing, shifting, or progressing. Whether it's a leaf blowing in the wind, a society fighting for justice, a musician performing a symphony, or the gears ticking inside a watch — whenever there is change, direction, and motion (physical or metaphorical), the word "movement" applies.

A quick summary of all the key meanings:

  • Physical: a change in position of a body or object
  • Whereabouts: a person's activities and locations over time
  • Social/Political: an organized collective effort to create change
  • Trend: a gradual, widespread shift in behavior or thinking
  • Artistic: a shared style or philosophy among creators
  • Musical: a self-contained section of a large composition
  • Medical: the passing of waste from the body (bowel movement)
  • Financial: a change in price or market value
  • Military: the repositioning of troops or supplies
  • Mechanical: the inner working mechanism of a clock or watch
10933:
Moxie means the guts, energy, and clever determination to face something hard without flinching — and to push through it with spirit.

If someone says "She has real moxie," they're paying a genuine compliment. They mean this person is bold, tough, and driven in a way that is admirable.
What Moxie Actually Means (The Full Picture)

Moxie isn't a single thing — it's a blend of three closely related qualities, and all three usually come together when you use the word:

1. Nerve and Courage
This is the willingness to do something difficult, risky, or uncomfortable without backing down. Not the cold, calculated bravery of a soldier following a plan — but the raw nerve of someone who sees a challenge and steps right up to it anyway, maybe even a little recklessly. It's the quality that makes someone speak up when everyone else stays quiet, or take on a task that most people would walk away from.

2. Energy and Drive
Moxie also implies a certain vitality — a lively, almost restless force that keeps a person going. Someone with moxie doesn't drag their feet. They attack problems with enthusiasm and hustle. There's a kind of fire to them.

3. Shrewdness and Street-Smart Know-How
The third layer is about figuring things out — having the practical cleverness to handle tough situations, especially when the odds aren't in your favor. This is less about book knowledge and more about the instinctive skill to navigate challenges, deal with difficult people, or come up with a solution under pressure.

Put all three together and you get the full meaning: moxie is the spirited, bold, resourceful quality of someone who refuses to be intimidated and keeps pushing forward with energy and smarts.
The Feeling and Personality of the Word

Moxie has a very specific emotional texture. It isn't the word you'd use for a calm, dignified kind of courage. It's scrappier and more colorful than that.

Think of the underdog who walks into a room full of more powerful, more experienced people — and instead of shrinking, holds their ground, speaks their mind, and somehow wins the room over. That's moxie.

Think of a young person with no connections, no resources, and no clear path — but who hustles, improvises, and claws their way forward anyway. That's moxie too.

It carries a slight sense of cheekiness or grit. The person with moxie isn't just brave — they're alive with it. There's personality in their bravery.

This will sharpen your understanding:

  • It's not quiet endurance. Simply suffering through hardship in silence isn't moxie. Moxie is active. It has forward momentum.
  • It's not arrogance. Moxie doesn't mean thinking you're the best. It means not letting fear or difficulty stop you — that's different from cockiness.
  • It's not just intelligence. A person can be brilliant but completely timid. Moxie is what pushes you to use your intelligence in the face of pressure.
  • It's not recklessness without purpose. Moxie has direction and determination behind it. It's not chaos.

The word is often used for:

  • A young professional who confidently challenges their boss's bad idea in a meeting, even though they're new.
  • A small business owner who keeps fighting to keep their shop alive against impossible odds.
  • A kid who stands up to a bully, even though the bully is bigger.
  • An athlete who comes back from behind and wins through sheer determination and hustle.
  • A journalist who chases a dangerous story that everyone else is afraid to touch.

• "It takes real moxie to walk into that negotiation with nothing but a good argument and win."
  • "I don't know how she does it — raising three kids, running a business, going to school. The woman has moxie."
  • "The rookie showed a lot of moxie out there tonight. She wasn't afraid of anyone."
  • "You've got to admire his moxie — most people would have quit by now."
  • "She walked right up to the CEO and pitched her idea on the spot. That kind of moxie is rare."

Moxie is an informal, colloquial word — the kind you'd use in everyday speech, casual writing, journalism, or storytelling. You wouldn't write it in a formal legal document or an academic paper. It has a warm, admiring, slightly old-fashioned American flavor to it. When someone uses it to describe you, it almost always means they respect you.

Moxie is the bold, energetic, scrappy combination of courage, drive, and cleverness that makes a person face hard things head-on — without backing down, without complaining, and often with a certain spirited flair.
10934:
"Muck about" is a British English idiom. It has two closely related but distinct meanings, and knowing both will help you use it correctly in any situation.

Meaning 1: To waste time or do things without any real purpose

When someone "mucks about," they spend time doing random, unproductive things instead of focusing on what they should be doing. There is no clear goal, no plan — just aimless activity.

Think of a student who sits down to study but ends up doodling, staring out the window, rearranging their pencils, and scrolling through their phone. That student is mucking about.

Examples:

  • "Stop mucking about and finish your homework!"
  • "We mucked about all afternoon and got nothing done."
  • "He's been mucking about in the kitchen for an hour and hasn't cooked a single thing."

Meaning 2: To play around in a carefree, silly, or fun way

This meaning is actually quite positive or at least neutral. It describes playful, lighthearted, often physical goofing around — the kind of thing children do when they're just having fun with no particular aim.

Examples:

  • "The kids spent the whole Saturday mucking about in the garden."
  • "We were just mucking about — it was a good laugh."
  • "I love mucking about with my friends on weekends."

So What's the Difference Between These Two Meanings?

The context tells you everything.

  • When someone should be doing something serious and is not, "mucking about" sounds like criticism — it means wasting time.
  • When there is no responsibility on the table, "mucking about" sounds casual and fun — it simply means playing around.

The phrase itself doesn't change. The tone and situation do.

Meaning 3: To treat someone carelessly or inconsiderately (often: "muck someone about")

There is a third, slightly different usage. When someone mucks you about, it means they mess you around, keep changing their plans, don't keep their word, or treat you without respect — causing you inconvenience or frustration.

Examples:

  • "The company kept mucking him about with his salary — first promising a raise, then denying it."
  • "Stop mucking me about and just tell me when you're arriving!"
  • "I'm tired of being mucked about by people who can't make up their minds."

This meaning is aimed at a person, not a task or time. It's about being treated unfairly or inconsistently.
Where Does the Phrase Come From?

The word "muck" originally meant dirt, filth, or animal dung — the kind of messy stuff you'd find on a farm. Over time, it came to be used more broadly to mean anything messy, dirty, or low in value. You "muck out" a stable (clean out the dung). You "muck up" a plan (ruin it). And you "muck about" when you're getting your hands dirty without any clear result — just making a mess of your time.

The word "about" here is used the way British English often uses it — meaning around, as in moving around without direction. Compare: "hanging about" (hanging around), "faffing about" (wasting time fussily), "messing about" (same as mucking about).

Yes, primarily. "Muck about" is overwhelmingly British and Australian. Americans are far less likely to use this phrase. Americans would more commonly say:

  • "mess around"
  • "fool around"
  • "goof off"
  • "jerk someone around" (for the third meaning)

If you are reading British novels, watching British TV shows, or talking to British or Australian people, you will hear "muck about" quite naturally. It is informal — not something you'd use in formal writing or professional settings.

These two are completely interchangeable. "Muck around" means exactly the same thing as "muck about" in all three meanings. Whether someone says one or the other is just a matter of personal habit or regional preference. You can use either one freely.

Understanding these similar phrases will deepen your feel for "muck about":

"Mess about / mess around" — Almost identical in meaning. "Stop messing about" = "Stop mucking about." This one is slightly more common in everyday British speech.

"Faff about / faff around" — Also British. Means to waste time in a flustered, disorganized, slightly anxious way. There's a hint of incompetence or indecisiveness that "muck about" doesn't always carry.

"Muck up" — To make a mess of something, to ruin or spoil it. "I mucked up the exam" means you did poorly or made a lot of mistakes. This is different from "muck about" — it's about ruining something, not just wasting time.

"Goof off" (American equivalent) — To avoid work and do unproductive things. Very close to Meaning 1 of "muck about."

Muck about (Meaning 1)Waste time; avoid doing what you should
Muck about (Meaning 2)Play around casually and cheerfully
Muck someone about (Meaning 3)Treat someone inconsiderately; mess them around
RegisterInformal British/Australian English
American equivalent"Mess around," "fool around," "goof off," "jerk someone around"
Same phrase, different word"Muck around" = exactly the same

• "We've been mucking about for hours — let's actually start the project." (wasting time)
  • "He was just mucking about in the pool with his younger brother." (playing)
  • "They keep mucking me about with the delivery date — first it was Monday, now it's Friday." (treating someone carelessly)

That's everything about "muck about." You now know its origins, all three meanings, how context shifts the tone, how it compares to similar expressions, and how it sits within British English. You're fully equipped to understand it wherever you encounter it — and to use it naturally yourself.
10935:
To muckrake means to actively search for and publicly expose wrongdoing, corruption, or scandalous behavior — especially by powerful people, politicians, businesses, or institutions.

When someone muckrakes, they are essentially digging through the "dirty" or hidden side of public life and dragging what they find into the open for everyone to see. Think of it as investigative truth-telling with a sharp, aggressive edge. The goal is always exposure.

Muckraking is almost always associated with journalism and investigative writing, though the word can apply to anyone performing this kind of deep, relentless digging into misconduct.

A person who muckrakes (called a muckraker) typically:

  • Investigates things that powerful people would strongly prefer to keep hidden
  • Digs persistently and thoroughly, often over a long period of time
  • Makes their findings public — through articles, books, documentaries, reports, etc.
  • Targets subjects like political corruption, corporate fraud, public health scandals, abuse of power, or social injustice
A Concrete Example to Make It Click

Imagine a journalist who suspects that a large pharmaceutical company has been hiding data showing that one of their drugs causes serious side effects. She doesn't just report a rumour — she spends two years quietly obtaining internal documents, interviewing whistleblowers, and cross-checking financial records. Then she publishes a bombshell series of articles that forces a government investigation and results in the drug being pulled from shelves.

That journalist has been muckraking.

The "muck" is the hidden wrongdoing. The "raking" is the act of rooting through it, turning it up, and bringing it to the surface.
The Tone of the Word — Does It Sound Positive or Negative?

This is where the word gets genuinely interesting, because it can be used both admiringly and critically, depending entirely on who is using it and why.

Used admiringly, muckraking sounds heroic — the brave act of a journalist who refuses to let the powerful escape accountability. In this sense, calling someone a muckraker is a compliment. It suggests they are doing the uncomfortable, dangerous, necessary work of holding institutions to account on behalf of ordinary people.

Used critically, muckraking carries a slightly dismissive or suspicious tone. It implies that the person is obsessively wallowing in filth and scandal for its own sake — stirring up controversy, sensationalising wrongdoing, or chasing dirt more out of a love of drama than a genuine commitment to public interest. In this sense, calling someone a muckraker is an insult, suggesting they are less a principled journalist and more a professional scandal-monger.

The key distinction is intent and purpose:

  • Is the exposure serving the public good? → Admirable muckraking
  • Is the digging driven mainly by sensationalism or personal agenda? → Questionable muckraking

In practice, the same act of journalism can be called muckraking by its supporters (proudly) and by its critics (dismissively) at exactly the same time. Context and the speaker's perspective determine the tone almost entirely.

To sharpen the definition, here is what separates muckraking from related concepts:

  • It is not regular news reporting. A reporter covering a press conference is not muckraking. Muckraking involves active, deep, independent digging — not simply relaying what officials say.
  • It is not gossip. Gossip is idle, informal chatter about private personal matters. Muckraking targets matters of genuine public concern — corruption, abuse of power, institutional wrongdoing — not merely embarrassing personal details.
  • It is not whistleblowing. A whistleblower is an insider who leaks information they have direct knowledge of. A muckraker is typically an outsider — usually a journalist — who uncovers information through investigation.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "The newspaper made its reputation by muckraking — exposing corrupt city officials for decades."
  • "Some politicians accused the documentary filmmaker of muckraking, claiming she was sensationalising isolated incidents."
  • "He muckraked his way through the financial industry, uncovering fraud that regulators had missed for years."
  • "She was one of the most celebrated muckrakers of her generation, feared by corporations and celebrated by the public."

To muckrake = to dig aggressively and persistently into hidden corruption or wrongdoing and expose it publicly, most often through journalism — an act that can be seen as either courageous truth-telling or obsessive scandal-hunting, depending on your point of view.
10936:
A muckraker is a person — almost always a journalist, writer, or reporter — who digs deep into society's darkest corners to expose corruption, injustice, wrongdoing, and abuse of power. They investigate things that powerful people, institutions, or corporations want kept hidden, and then bring those ugly truths to the public's attention.

Think of it this way: "muck" is dirt and filth. A muckraker is someone who isn't afraid to get their hands dirty sifting through that filth — not for personal gain, but to hold up what they find and show it to the world.

A muckraker doesn't just report the news as it comes. They go searching for it — spending months, sometimes years, investigating a single issue. Their work typically involves:

  • Interviewing sources who are afraid to speak openly
  • Reviewing documents, financial records, and internal files
  • Going undercover to witness wrongdoing firsthand
  • Connecting dots that powerful people hope no one ever connects

Their targets are typically institutions with power: governments, corporations, police departments, hospitals, banks — any organization capable of doing widespread harm while hiding behind respectability.

This is important: the word "muckraker" is slightly double-edged, meaning it can be used both admiringly and critically, depending on who is using it and why.

When used admiringly: A muckraker is a brave, public-spirited truth-teller. They are the watchdog of democracy, the person willing to speak uncomfortable truths to protect ordinary people from powerful wrongdoers. In this sense, calling someone a muckraker is a compliment — it suggests courage, persistence, and a commitment to justice.

When used dismissively or critically: Those in power — especially those being investigated — sometimes use "muckraker" as an insult. They use it to suggest that the journalist is a troublemaker, an obsessive, someone who wallows in scandal and negativity, or who exaggerates problems just to sell stories. In this sense, the word implies someone who only looks for dirt, even where there isn't any, or who has a cynical, negative view of the world.

In everyday modern usage, the word leans more positive than negative. Most people use it to describe a journalist who does brave, important investigative work.

To fully understand the word, you need to know a small piece of history — not where the word came from, but why it matters.

In the early 1900s in the United States, a generation of journalists took it upon themselves to expose the rampant corruption of that era. Corporations were poisoning food, exploiting workers in horrific conditions, bribing politicians, and destroying competition through illegal monopolies — all while the public had no idea. These journalists decided to investigate and write about it in magazines and books that millions of Americans read.

Some landmark examples:

  • Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle (1906), a book that revealed the stomach-turning, unsanitary conditions in the American meatpacking industry — rotting meat, dangerous chemicals, and workers losing fingers and falling into vats. It shocked the nation and directly led to food safety laws.
  • Ida Tarbell spent years methodically investigating the Standard Oil Company, owned by John D. Rockefeller, the most powerful corporation in America. She published a detailed series exposing how Standard Oil used illegal tactics to crush competition and overcharge consumers. Her work eventually led to the company being broken up by the government.
  • Jacob Riis went into New York City's poorest slums, photographed them, and wrote about the miserable, overcrowded, disease-ridden conditions that the wealthy classes preferred not to think about. His work moved the public and triggered real reforms.

These people became the original, definitive muckrakers. Their work showed what the word truly means at its best: using journalism as a tool of justice.

The tradition continues. Today's muckrakers might be investigative journalists at major newspapers, independent reporters, documentary filmmakers, or even solo writers. Some famous modern examples of muckraking-style work include:

  • The Washington Post's exposure of the Watergate scandal in the 1970s, which brought down President Nixon
  • The Boston Globe's investigation into the Catholic Church's cover-up of widespread child abuse by priests (featured in the film Spotlight)
  • Investigative reporting that exposed the Panama Papers — a massive leak of financial documents revealing how the world's ultra-wealthy hide money in secret offshore accounts

In every case, the pattern is the same: a powerful entity doing wrong, someone willing to dig until the truth is undeniable, and a public that deserved to know.

• "She spent two years as a muckraker, eventually publishing a report that led to the CEO's resignation."
  • "The senator dismissed the journalist as a muckraker with an agenda."
  • "The golden age of muckraking changed American politics forever."

The related verb is to muckrake, and the activity itself is called muckraking.

A muckraker is an investigative journalist or writer who bravely digs into corruption and wrongdoing — especially by the powerful — and exposes it publicly, often at great personal or professional risk, with the goal of informing the public and driving change.
10937:
Muckraking is the practice of digging deep into powerful institutions, corporations, or governments to uncover hidden wrongdoing, corruption, or injustice, and then bringing that information to the public's attention. It is a form of investigative journalism done specifically in the public interest.

Think of it this way: most news reports what is already visible. Muckraking goes hunting for what powerful people are actively trying to keep hidden.

Not all reporting qualifies as muckraking. Three things define it:

1. It targets power. Muckraking always punches upward. It goes after people, companies, or systems that have significant wealth, authority, or influence — precisely because those are the ones with something to hide and the resources to hide it. A story about a neighborhood dispute is not muckraking. A story exposing that a pharmaceutical company knowingly sold a dangerous drug while hiding the evidence absolutely is.

2. It involves deep, original investigation. A muckraker does not simply report what they were told or what was handed to them. They dig. They read thousands of documents, interview dozens of sources, follow money trails, and sometimes spend months or even years on a single story. The wrongdoing would likely remain buried if the journalist hadn't gone looking for it.

3. It serves the public good. The goal of muckraking is not gossip or entertainment. It is exposure that leads to awareness, accountability, and ideally reform. The muckraker wants society to see something it needs to see.
Where the Word Comes From (Historically, Not Linguistically)

The term was launched into popular use in 1906 by U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt. He was referencing a character from a famous old book who was so obsessed with raking through filth on the floor that he could never look upward toward anything better. Roosevelt used the term as mild criticism — he respected investigative reporters but worried that some were so focused on exposing darkness that they never acknowledged anything good.

Here's the irony: the journalists he was describing actually embraced the label. They wore it as a badge of honor. If raking through the muck of corruption was what it took to clean up society, they were proud to do it. And the name stuck.

Muckraking as a recognizable movement exploded in the United States during the Progressive Era (roughly 1890s–1920s), a time when industrialization had created enormously powerful corporations and deeply corrupt city and federal governments — and ordinary citizens were suffering as a result.

Some landmark examples from this period:

Ida Tarbell spent years investigating Standard Oil, the massive oil monopoly controlled by John D. Rockefeller. She published a detailed, meticulously researched series of articles exposing how the company used illegal and ruthless tactics to crush all competition. Her work contributed directly to the U.S. Supreme Court breaking Standard Oil apart in 1911.

Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle (1906), a novel based on deep undercover investigation into the meatpacking industry in Chicago. He described in vivid, nauseating detail the horrifying sanitary conditions in which the food Americans ate was being processed — workers falling into vats, rat droppings mixed into the product, diseased animals being processed anyway. The public outcry was immediate and massive, and it led directly to the passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act — legislation that is still the foundation of food safety regulation in the United States today.

Lincoln Steffens investigated and exposed the systematic political corruption happening inside American cities, showing how city governments were essentially being run by criminal networks of politicians and businessmen who fed off each other at the public's expense.

Nellie Bly had herself committed to a psychiatric institution by pretending to be mentally ill, and then reported from the inside on the horrifying and abusive conditions patients were subjected to. Her reporting led to a significant increase in the budget for psychiatric care and reforms in how patients were treated.

These weren't small stories. These investigations changed laws, toppled monopolies, and improved lives on a national scale.

Muckraking never went away — it evolved. Modern examples include:

Investigative reporting on corporate wrongdoing — such as journalists uncovering that a major company had been dumping toxic waste while publicly claiming to be environmentally responsible.

Political corruption investigations — reporting that traces how public officials secretly directed government contracts to their own business interests.

Institutional abuse stories — investigations into how systems meant to protect people (churches, schools, hospitals, police forces) instead harbored and covered up abuse.

The #MeToo investigations that exposed Harvey Weinstein and others involved classic muckraking: years of hidden wrongdoing, powerful people using money and influence to keep victims silent, and journalists doing painstaking investigative work over many months to bring the truth to light.
The Word's Connotation — Positive or Negative?

This depends on who is using it and in what context.

Used positively or neutrally: Most of the time, calling someone a muckraker or calling journalism muckraking is respectful — it implies serious, meaningful, socially important investigative work. Many journalists consider it a compliment.

Used negatively: Sometimes critics use the word dismissively to suggest that a journalist is simply digging up dirt for the sake of scandal, sensationalism, or to harm a person's reputation, without genuine public interest justification. In this usage, the implication is that the journalist is wallowing in filth rather than serving any noble purpose.

The difference almost always comes down to motive and substance: Is the investigation uncovering something that genuinely affects the public? Or is it just embarrassing someone powerful for the sake of it?

If you had to explain muckraking in two sentences:

Muckraking is investigative journalism that specifically hunts for hidden corruption, wrongdoing, or injustice in powerful institutions and brings it to public light. Its purpose is not just to inform, but to provoke accountability and spark real-world change.

"The senator tried to dismiss the newspaper's investigation as muckraking, but the documents it published were impossible to ignore."

"A long tradition of muckraking in American journalism has led to some of the most important pieces of legislation in the country's history."

"The documentary was pure muckraking — it revealed how the company had knowingly mislead regulators for over a decade."
10938:
A muddle is a state of confusion, disorder, or mess — where things (or thoughts) are all mixed up, tangled together, and hard to make sense of. Think of it as a situation or a mental state where nothing is clear, organized, or in its right place.

The single most important phrase to remember is: "in a muddle." That is how this word is most naturally used.

"Muddle" as a noun works in two broad ways:

1. A muddle of things (physical disorder)
This is when objects, papers, tasks, or information are jumbled up and disorganized — a messy, tangled pile where you can't easily find or sort anything.

"There was a muddle of old letters, keys, and receipts on the table."

Here, "muddle" points to a physical mix-up — things that belong in separate places have all ended up together in a confusing heap.

2. A muddle in someone's mind or a situation (mental/situational confusion)
This is when a person can't think clearly, or when a situation has become so tangled and unclear that no one knows what's happening or what to do next.

"After reading the instructions three times, he was still in a muddle."
"The whole event ended up in a muddle — no one knew who was supposed to do what."

Here, "muddle" captures that foggy, lost, "I don't understand what's going on" feeling.
What Makes a Muddle a Muddle (and Not Something Else)

This is important. A muddle is not just any mess or confusion. It has a specific character:

  • It is accidental, not deliberate. A muddle happens because things went wrong on their own, not because someone planned it that way. It suggests carelessness or bad luck, not sabotage.
  • It is mild-to-moderate, not catastrophic. A muddle is messy and frustrating, but it is not a disaster. You wouldn't call a war or a destroyed city "a muddle." It's the kind of confusion you can, in principle, sort out — it just takes effort.
  • It is tangled, not simply empty. A muddle implies there is something there — information, tasks, objects — but they are all mixed up together. It's not about a lack of things; it's about things being in the wrong order or all clumped together confusingly.
  • It often implies mild incompetence or poor management. When someone says a project ended up "in a muddle," there's a quiet suggestion that someone didn't handle things well. It's a gentle criticism.
The Feeling of Being "In a Muddle"

To be in a muddle means you feel mentally foggy, confused, and unsure of where to start. Imagine waking up and forgetting what day it is, having three urgent tasks in front of you with no idea which to tackle first, and your notes being scattered everywhere. That entire experience — the fog, the disorder, the lostness — is being "in a muddle."

"She had so many deadlines at once that she was completely in a muddle."

Like many English words, "muddle" can be used with different intensities:

  • "a bit of a muddle" — a mild, minor confusion; almost affectionate
  • "a complete muddle" — a thorough, serious state of disorder
  • "a right muddle" — (especially British English) a real, significant mess

The word is particularly common in British English, where it is a natural, everyday word. It can even be used in a slightly affectionate or humorous way, especially when describing a friendly, harmless kind of disorder.

"Oh, Grandma's handbag is always a wonderful muddle of tissues, mints, and coins."
The Difference Between a Muddle and Similar Words

Understanding what a word is not makes its meaning sharper.

  • Muddle vs. chaos — Chaos is extreme, overwhelming, often violent disorder. A muddle is smaller, quieter, and more manageable. A battlefield is chaotic. A disorganized desk is a muddle.
  • Muddle vs. mess — A mess is primarily about physical untidiness. A muddle is about confusion — things being mixed up in a way that makes them hard to understand or navigate. A messy room is not necessarily a muddle; a muddle of arrangements for a party means the plans themselves are unclear and tangled.
  • Muddle vs. mix-up — A mix-up is a specific mistake where things were confused (e.g., names or orders were swapped). A muddle is a broader state of ongoing confusion, not just a single error.

A muddle is a state of confusion and disorder — either in the physical arrangement of things, in someone's thinking, or in how a situation has developed. It is accidental, mild-to-moderate in severity, and suggests things are all tangled together in a way that's hard to sort out. It does not imply destruction or extreme chaos — just frustrating, fixable disorder. The phrase "in a muddle" is its most natural home.
10939: At the heart of every meaning of muddle is the idea of a confused, disordered mess — whether that mess is in your mind, in physical objects, or in the way you're doing something. Think of it as the opposite of clarity and order. When something is muddled, it is jumbled, unclear, and tangled up.

1. To confuse someone's mind

This is perhaps the most common meaning. To muddle someone means to make them confused, mixed up, or unable to think clearly. The confusion here is genuine — the person genuinely cannot sort things out in their head.

"All these instructions have completely muddled me."
(= I can't make sense of them. My thinking is confused.)

"Stop interrupting me — you're muddling my thoughts."

Notice the feeling here: it's not a gentle confusion. It's a feeling of your mind being stirred up like muddy water, where you can't see clearly.

2. To mix things up or confuse one thing with another

Here, muddle means to mix things up incorrectly, or to mistake one thing for another. The things could be physical objects placed in the wrong order, or ideas and facts that have gotten tangled together.

"Someone has muddled all my files. Nothing is in the right folder."

"She keeps muddling the names of her two nephews."
(= She mixes them up and uses the wrong name for each.)

In this sense, the word captures the idea of a careless, disordered mixing — not a deliberate, careful combining, but a messy, accidental jumbling.

3. To handle something in a confused, disorganised, or clumsy way

When someone muddles something, they deal with it badly and without a clear plan — not necessarily making a catastrophic mistake, but bumbling through it incompetently or carelessly.

"The government completely muddled the crisis response."
(= They handled it in a disorganised, unclear, ineffective way.)

4. (Specialised) To crush ingredients gently

In cocktail-making and cooking, to muddle means to gently crush or press soft ingredients — like mint leaves, fruit, or sugar — at the bottom of a glass or bowl, in order to release their juices and flavours.

"Muddle the mint leaves with a little sugar before adding the rum."

This meaning shares the same root spirit as the others: you are working something over physically, breaking it down.

These are essential because native speakers use them constantly.

Muddle through
To barely succeed at something by fumbling your way forward — without a clear plan, making mistakes, but somehow getting to the end. It implies survival, not elegance.

"I don't really know how to use this software, but I'll muddle through."
(= I'll manage somehow, even if it's messy.)

This phrase often carries a slightly affectionate or self-deprecating tone. The British especially use it to describe getting by without great skill or preparation.

Muddle along
Similar to "muddle through," but used for an ongoing situation rather than a single task. It means to continue in a disorganised, directionless, but not completely failing way — just drifting along without real purpose or plan.

"The department has just been muddling along for years with no real leadership."

Muddle up
To confuse two or more things with each other, or to put things in the wrong order. Very close to Meaning #2 above, but the "up" makes the action feel more complete — a thorough mixing-up.

"I always muddle up 'affect' and 'effect'."
"Who muddled up all the books on the shelf?"

The phrase "get muddled up" is also very common:

"I got completely muddled up trying to follow the map."
(= I became thoroughly confused.)
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is important and often left out of dictionary definitions.

"Muddle" is not a harsh or dramatic word. It doesn't suggest a disaster or a crisis. It suggests something more like a soft, helpless, unhappy confusion — a state of disorder that is frustrating but not catastrophic. When something is muddled, it feels foggy, tangled, and unclear rather than smashed or broken.

Compare:

  • "She destroyed the argument" — forceful, deliberate
  • "She muddled the argument" — confused it, made it unclear, lost the thread

Muddling is often accidental or the result of poor thinking, not malice. Someone who muddles something is usually not doing it on purpose — they are simply confused themselves, or careless.

If you muddle...It means...
A personYou confuse them mentally
Things (objects/ideas)You mix them up wrongly, confuse one for another
A task or situationYou handle it in a disorganised, clumsy way
IngredientsYou crush them gently to release flavour
Through somethingYou barely manage to get through it
AlongYou drift forward in a directionless, inefficient way
Up two thingsYou mix them up / confuse them with each other

The word "muddle" is wonderfully expressive. It almost sounds like what it means — soft, mixed up, a little helpless. Once you have the central image of murky, stirred-up water where nothing is clear, every use of this word will make immediate sense to you.
